title: Preorder Traversal
description: Given a binary tree in level-order form using -1 for nulls, print its preorder traversal.
inputFormat: An integer n representing number of level-order entries
n space-separated integers with -1 for null
intendedApproachSummary: Visit root, then recurse on left subtree, then recurse on right subtree.
wrongApproachHints: Preorder is not left-root-right.
You must stop recursion at null nodes.
hints: Base case is root == null.
Print before recursive calls.

examples.explanation: Preorder visits each node before its children.

title: Inorder Traversal
description: Given a binary tree in level-order form using -1 for nulls, print its inorder traversal.
inputFormat: n level-order values with -1 for null
intendedApproachSummary: Recurse on left subtree, visit root, then recurse on right subtree.
wrongApproachHints: Do not print the root before the left subtree in inorder.
hints: The root visit happens between the two recursive calls.

examples.explanation: Inorder visits left, root, right.

title: Postorder Traversal
description: Given a binary tree in level-order form using -1 for nulls, print its postorder traversal.
inputFormat: n level-order values with -1 for null
intendedApproachSummary: Recurse on left subtree, then right subtree, and print the root last.
wrongApproachHints: Postorder prints the root after both subtrees are complete.
hints: Base case remains root == null.
Print after both recursive calls.

examples.explanation: Postorder visits children before the parent.

title: Level Order Traversal
description: Given a binary tree in level-order form using -1 for nulls, print the nodes level by level from left to right.
inputFormat: n level-order values with -1 for null
intendedApproachSummary: Use a queue and repeatedly process the current front node, pushing its non-null children.
wrongApproachHints: This is a queue problem, not a recursive DFS order.
hints: Start with the root in the queue.
Pop front, print it, then push children.

examples.explanation: Level order visits breadth-first.

title: Height of Binary Tree
description: Given a binary tree in level-order form using -1 for nulls, print its height measured in number of nodes on the longest root-to-leaf path.
inputFormat: n level-order values with -1 for null
intendedApproachSummary: Height(root) = 1 + max(height(left), height(right)); height(null) = 0.
wrongApproachHints: Do not confuse level count with edge count unless the problem says so.
hints: Base case for null is 0.
Combine child answers with max.

examples.explanation: The longest path has 3 nodes.

title: Diameter of Binary Tree
description: Given a binary tree in level-order form using -1 for nulls, print its diameter measured in number of edges on the longest path between any two nodes.
inputFormat: n level-order values with -1 for null
edgeCases: Longest path may not go through root
intendedApproachSummary: While computing subtree heights, update a global best with leftHeight + rightHeight.
wrongApproachHints: Do not recompute heights separately for every node.
hints: Return heights from recursion.
Update diameter before returning the current height.

examples.explanation: The longest path is 4 -> 2 -> 1 -> 3.

title: Check Balanced Binary Tree
description: Given a binary tree in level-order form using -1 for nulls, print Balanced if every node has left and right subtree heights differing by at most 1; otherwise print Not Balanced.
inputFormat: n level-order values with -1 for null
intendedApproachSummary: Return subtree heights, but return a failure marker as soon as an imbalance is found.
wrongApproachHints: Checking only the root height difference is not enough.
Repeated standalone height calls make the solution O(n^2).
hints: Use -1 as an imbalance marker if you like.
Propagate imbalance upward immediately.

examples.explanation: Every node still satisfies the balance condition.

title: Search in BST
description: Given a BST in level-order form using -1 for nulls and a target value, print Found if the target exists, otherwise print Not Found.
inputFormat: n level-order values with -1 for null
intendedApproachSummary: Compare target with the current node value and move left or right accordingly.
wrongApproachHints: Do not search both subtrees blindly; use the BST property.
hints: If target < node.val, go left.
If target > node.val, go right.

examples.explanation: 5 lies in the right subtree of 4 and the left subtree of 6.

functionContract.javaSignature: public boolean searchBST(TreeNode root, int target)

title: Left View of Binary Tree
description: Given a binary tree in level-order form using -1 for nulls, print the left view of the tree.
inputFormat: n level-order values with -1 for null
intendedApproachSummary: Use level-order traversal and record the first node processed at each level.
wrongApproachHints: Do not print all nodes from every level.
The left view keeps one representative per level.
hints: Before processing a level, note the queue size.
The first node in each level is part of the answer.

examples.explanation: From the left side, these are the first visible nodes per level.

title: Insert into BST
description: Given a BST in level-order form using -1 for nulls and a value x, insert x into the BST and print its inorder traversal.
inputFormat: n level-order values with -1 for null
edgeCases: Insert as leaf on either side
intendedApproachSummary: Descend left or right until a null child is found, then attach the new node there.
wrongApproachHints: Do not rebuild the whole tree from scratch.
Preserve the BST property during insertion.
hints: Compare x with current node value.
Stop when the correct child link is null.

examples.explanation: 8 becomes the right child of 7.

functionContract.javaSignature: public TreeNode insertBST(TreeNode root, int x)

title: Delete Node in BST
description: Given a BST in level-order form using -1 for nulls and a key, delete the key from the BST and print its inorder traversal.
inputFormat: n level-order values with -1 for null
intendedApproachSummary: Handle the three delete cases carefully. For two children, replace with inorder successor or predecessor and delete that replacement node recursively.
wrongApproachHints: You cannot just drop a node with children.
Be careful not to lose subtrees when reconnecting.
hints: Find the successor in the right subtree.
Delete the successor after copying its value.

examples.explanation: 3 is replaced while preserving BST order.

functionContract.javaSignature: public TreeNode deleteBST(TreeNode root, int key)

title: Top View of Binary Tree
description: Given a binary tree in level-order form using -1 for nulls, print its top view from leftmost visible node to rightmost.
inputFormat: n level-order values with -1 for null
edgeCases: Multiple nodes share the same horizontal distance
intendedApproachSummary: Run BFS while tracking horizontal distance. The first node seen at a distance belongs to the top view.
wrongApproachHints: DFS alone can easily take a deeper node before a shallower one.
Only the first node per horizontal distance should be kept.
hints: Store pairs of node and horizontal distance in the queue.
Use an ordered map for final left-to-right printing.

examples.explanation: These nodes are visible from the top.

title: Optimal Lowest Common Ancestor
description: Given a binary tree in level-order form using -1 for nulls and two node values p and q known to exist, print the value of their lowest common ancestor using the optimal single-pass recursive strategy.
inputFormat: n level-order values with -1 for null
edgeCases: One node is ancestor of the other
intendedApproachSummary: Return root if it matches p or q. Recurse into both subtrees; if both return non-null, root is the LCA. Otherwise bubble the non-null side upward.
wrongApproachHints: The first matched target is not always the final answer.
You need information from both sides.
hints: Base cases are root == null or root.val == p/q.
If both left and right answers are non-null, return root.

examples.explanation: 5 and 1 split at root 3.

functionContract.javaSignature: public int lowestCommonAncestor(TreeNode root, int p, int q)
functionContract.cppSignature: int lowestCommonAncestor(TreeNode* root, int p, int q)

title: Build Tree from Preorder and Inorder
description: Given preorder and inorder traversals of a binary tree with distinct values, construct the tree and print its postorder traversal.
outputFormat: Print postorder traversal of the reconstructed tree
intendedApproachSummary: The preorder front gives the root. Use an inorder index map to split left and right subtree ranges recursively.
wrongApproachHints: Repeated linear search in inorder makes the solution too slow.
You must respect subtree boundaries while recursing.
hints: Keep a preorder index that advances as roots are created.
Map inorder values to indices for O(1) splits.

examples.explanation: That is the postorder traversal of the reconstructed tree.

functionContract.javaSignature: public TreeNode buildTree(int[] preorder, int[] inorder)

title: Serialize Binary Tree (Level Order)
description: Given a binary tree in level-order form using -1 for nulls, serialize it again using level order with # for null nodes, trimming only the unnecessary trailing null markers.
inputFormat: n level-order values with -1 for null
outputFormat: Print the serialized tokens separated by spaces
edgeCases: Sparse tree needs internal null markers
Do not keep useless trailing null markers forever
intendedApproachSummary: Use a queue for BFS and emit # whenever a missing child is encountered. After traversal, trim only trailing # markers.
wrongApproachHints: Skipping null markers entirely loses the structure.
Only trailing null markers may be removed safely.
hints: Push both children of a non-null node into the queue.
Track output tokens and trim from the back at the end.

examples.explanation: The null children of node 2 must be preserved to keep the shape.

title: Maximum Root-to-Leaf Path Sum
description: Given a binary tree in level-order form using -1 for nulls, print the maximum sum on any path that starts at the root and ends at a leaf. Node values may be negative.
inputFormat: n level-order values with -1 for null
outputFormat: Print the maximum root-to-leaf path sum
intendedApproachSummary: Return the best downward path sum from each node by taking the larger child contribution and adding the current node value.
wrongApproachHints: Do not sum both children when returning to the parent.
Handle negative values carefully instead of assuming every child helps.
hints: A leaf returns its own value.
At each node, choose the better child contribution before adding the current value.

examples.explanation: The best root-to-leaf path is 1 -> 3 -> 6.

title: Leaf Traversal of Binary Tree
description: Given a binary tree in level-order form using -1 for nulls, print all leaf nodes from left to right.
inputFormat: n level-order values with -1 for null
edgeCases: Single-node tree is itself a leaf
Sparse tree with leaves at different depths
intendedApproachSummary: Use DFS and record a node only when both children are null.
wrongApproachHints: Do not print non-leaf nodes that happen to be on the outer edges.
Do not miss a right leaf just because there is no left child.
hints: A leaf is a node with left == null and right == null.
Visit left subtree before right subtree to preserve order.

examples.explanation: These are the leaves from left to right.

title: Boundary Traversal of Binary Tree
description: Given a binary tree in level-order form using -1 for nulls, print its boundary traversal as root, left boundary excluding leaves, all leaves left to right, and right boundary excluding leaves in reverse.
inputFormat: n level-order values with -1 for null
edgeCases: Root-only tree should print root once
Skewed tree should not duplicate nodes between boundary and leaf passes
intendedApproachSummary: Collect left boundary, then leaves, then right boundary in reverse while skipping leaves in the boundary phases.
wrongApproachHints: Do not add leaves during both the boundary walk and the leaf DFS.
The right boundary must be appended in reverse order.
hints: Write a small isLeaf helper first.
Prefer left child on the left boundary and right child on the right boundary, with fallback to the other side.

examples.explanation: This follows left boundary, leaves, then reversed right boundary without duplicates.

title: Vertical Traversal with Ordered Buckets
description: Given a binary tree in level-order form using -1 for nulls, print its vertical traversal from leftmost column to rightmost. Within a column, nodes should appear from top to bottom, and if two nodes share the same row and column, print the smaller value first.
inputFormat: n level-order values with -1 for null
outputFormat: Print one line per column with values in traversal order
edgeCases: Multiple nodes share the same row and column
Sparse trees with negative column indices
intendedApproachSummary: Run BFS or DFS while tracking row and column, bucket nodes by column, then sort each bucket by row and value before printing columns from smallest to largest.
wrongApproachHints: Column tracking alone is not enough when two nodes land at the same depth.
Do not rely on insertion order when value tie-breaking is required.
hints: Store triples like (column, row, value).
Use an ordered map for columns and sort each column bucket by row first, then value.

examples.explanation: Columns are emitted left to right, with row/value ordering preserved within each column.

title: Root-to-Leaf Paths as Strings
description: Given a binary tree in level-order form using -1 for nulls, return every root-to-leaf path as a string joined by -> in left-to-right order.
inputFormat: n level-order values with -1 for null
outputFormat: Print one path string per line
edgeCases: Single-node tree returns one path with only the root
Skewed tree has only one root-to-leaf path
intendedApproachSummary: Use DFS, carry the current path text or node list downward, and emit a path only when a leaf node is reached.
wrongApproachHints: Do not print partial paths for internal nodes.
Do not let one branch overwrite the path built for a sibling branch.
hints: A leaf is the moment to push the completed path into the answer list.
Pass the current path forward with each recursive call.

examples.explanation: The two root-to-leaf paths are 1->2->5 and 1->3.

title: Search Value in Binary Tree
description: Given a binary tree in level-order form using -1 for nulls and a target value, print Found if the target exists anywhere in the tree, otherwise print Not Found.
inputFormat: n level-order values with -1 for null
edgeCases: Target exists only in the right subtree
intendedApproachSummary: Check the current node, then recurse into left and right subtrees until one side reports success.
wrongApproachHints: This is a general binary tree, so you cannot choose one direction by value ordering.
Do not stop after only checking the left subtree.
hints: Base case: null means the target is not found here.
If current node is not the target, either subtree may still contain it.

examples.explanation: The value 5 exists in the left subtree.

functionContract.javaSignature: public boolean containsValue(TreeNode root, int target)

title: Root to Node Path
description: Given a binary tree in level-order form using -1 for nulls and a target value known to exist, print the path from root to that target.
inputFormat: n level-order values with -1 for null
outputFormat: Print the root-to-target path values separated by spaces
edgeCases: Target sits deep in only one branch
intendedApproachSummary: Carry the current path during DFS, keep it when the target is found, and backtrack when a branch fails.
wrongApproachHints: Do not keep failed branch nodes in the final path.
Finding the target is not enough unless the path state is preserved.
hints: Push before recursive calls and pop when a branch does not work.
The first successful branch determines the path.

examples.explanation: These nodes form the path from the root to 4.

functionContract.javaSignature: public List<Integer> rootToNodePath(TreeNode root, int target)

title: LCA Using Paths
description: Given a binary tree in level-order form using -1 for nulls and two node values p and q known to exist, compute their lowest common ancestor by building both root-to-node paths first.
inputFormat: n level-order values with -1 for null
edgeCases: One node is ancestor of the other
The paths diverge right below the root
intendedApproachSummary: Construct root-to-node paths for both targets, then walk both arrays from the front until they diverge. The last common node is the LCA.
wrongApproachHints: Comparing from the leaf side does not identify the lowest shared ancestor correctly.
Both paths must start from the root.
hints: Reuse your root-to-node path logic twice.
Track the last equal node while both paths match.

examples.explanation: The two paths first diverge after the root, so the answer is 3.

functionContract.cppSignature: int lowestCommonAncestorUsingPaths(TreeNode* root, int p, int q)

title: Count Targets in Subtree
description: Given a binary tree in level-order form using -1 for nulls and two target values p and q, return how many of those target values appear in the current tree.
inputFormat: n level-order values with -1 for null
edgeCases: Both targets are in the same subtree
intendedApproachSummary: Return the sum of left count, right count, and a local match count for the current node.
wrongApproachHints: You cannot keep only one subtree result if both sides may contain targets.
Do not forget to count the current node itself.
hints: A null node contributes zero.
Each recursive call should return a count to its parent.

examples.explanation: Both 5 and 4 are present in the tree.

functionContract.javaSignature: public int countTargetsInSubtree(TreeNode root, int p, int q)
functionContract.cppSignature: int countTargetsInSubtree(TreeNode* root, int p, int q)

title: Count Leaf Nodes
description: Given a binary tree in level-order form using -1 for nulls, count how many leaf nodes it contains.
inputFormat: n level-order values with -1 for null
outputFormat: Print the number of leaf nodes
edgeCases: A single-node tree has exactly one leaf
Sparse trees can still have leaves on both sides
intendedApproachSummary: Use DFS. If a node has no left and right child, count it as one leaf. Otherwise return the leaf counts from both subtrees.
wrongApproachHints: Do not count null children as leaves.
A node with one child is not a leaf.
hints: A leaf has left == null and right == null.
Recursive answers from left and right subtrees should be added together.
